Law is order, which means location.
See Corollary 1 to The Nomos of the Earth.
The two hunters on p. 23 of Land and Sea are mythical, and not merely mythology. For all the talk about myth that has gone on for years, I know only one man who truly realizes myth as a poet:
In him, the dissolution and self-dissolution of the great philosophy of German idealism releases theogonic transformations.
Thirty-two years ago I published a small book on Däubler’s Northern Lights, which I had pulped in 1925.
Today he confronts me again with immense power. And the little book contains completely different things from what I thought it contained at the time.
Däubler, incidentally, was the first to make use of the magic in the word “space,” long before the Expressionists and before Rilke.
But, however, and in spite of everything:
I know the dear Germans already, etc.
Beware of every microphone that carries your voice into the wrong public sphere.
Every amplifier of sound is a falsifier of meaning.
World public opinion is the deception of the world.
What belongs to the world belongs to the devil. That is as true again today as it was in the year 63, in the time of Nero, Seneca, and the Apostle Paul.

Today the beautiful Christian forms of creaturely life developed by the Middle Ages have once again been completely abolished and assimilated away. But beware also of the false echo produced in the winding vaults of the catacombs.

Last night I almost succumbed again to the impatience of justice when I reread Francisco de Vitoria: the seven tituli idonei et non idonei, the valid and invalid titles, and once again recognized the horrifying abuse made of his doctrine of just war.
Especially the five Dubia circa justitiam belli, doubts concerning the justice of war, and the nine Dubiosa quantum liceat in bello justo, doubts concerning how much is permitted in a just war.
Anyone who speaks of just war without showing that all these dubia and dubiosa have become part of his practical, moral, and historical consciousness no longer has any authority on his side.
The ideological fraud involved in exploiting and using all these doubts becomes all the clearer.
The trick is one that Francisco de Vitoria himself already employs:
omnia cedunt in favorem et jus justum bellum gerentium.
Everything gives way in favour of those who wage a just war and of the rights they claim through it.
With the help of this principle, even the otherwise so cautious Vitoria allows captured war booty not to be counted against claims for reparations and requisitions:
si licite sunt capta, puto quod non sunt obnoxia restitutioni.
If they were lawfully captured, I think they are not subject to restitution. So says the great theologian in De jure belli, second doubt concerning how much is permitted in a just war.
So much is permitted in a just war!!
Perhaps this sentence can help me identify my own peccatum, my own sin, and thereby answer the question that has tormented me for years:
Why does everything I say provoke such inexplicable hostility?
What terrible thing have I done?

J’ai montré la porte secrète de ce sanctuaire écarté où se jugent les perplexités de la justice et tous les problèmes, pour lesquels Thémis n’a pas de balance: car si on les montre, l’avide intérêt et tous les sophismes des passions forcent bientôt la porte et violent la conscience dans son dernier asile.
I showed the secret door of that secluded sanctuary where the perplexities of justice are judged, together with all those problems for which Themis has no scales.
For once that door is shown, greedy self-interest and all the sophistries of passion soon force their way through it and violate conscience in its final refuge.
I am still thinking about Francisco de Vitoria.
About his seven tituli non idonei, invalid titles, and seven tituli idonei, valid titles.
About the five dubia circa justitiam belli, doubts concerning the justice of war. And the nine doubts concerning “how much is permitted in a just war.”

Then the impatience of justice takes hold of me for days at a time. This is the form of despair that comes with my profession as a jurist. But I do not want to die from it, as poor Max Weber did, whom I watched die from it in 1920.
At the time I thought it was very foolish to let oneself be consumed by such a thing and literally waste away from it.
Now I am receiving the lesson that has meanwhile become due.
Do you consider it completely impossible to interest a Catholic moral theologian in the subject of “legality”?
Which religious order would even be suitable?
When I consider Vitoria’s attitude and his effect, I become frightened of the Dominicans.
I am now afraid that my chapter on Vitoria in the Nomos is far too gentle and considerate, almost concealing the issue, and that it therefore loses its force.

What I say there, very quietly, about Nys, James Brown Scott—and therefore about Jackson—is in substance every bit as serious as what Augustin Cochin, Valléry-Radot, and the earlier Bernanos, before he became weak, said and did.
The Dominicans regard Vitoria as one of their household saints and as a matter of institutional prestige.
What is a layman supposed to do against that?
Ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis.
Where you have no power, desire nothing.

I could demonstrate from Vitoria—and from his own words, especially the five Dubia circa bellum justum and the nine doubts concerning “how much is permitted in a just war”—that the just war is total war.
Have I already asked you about Höffner’s book on Vitoria, which bears the confidence-inspiring title Christianity and Human Dignity?
I do not know it yet.
In my experience so far, nine tenths of everything being written about Vitoria today is an outrageous fraud.
From a scholarly point of view, pure rubbish.
Nothing but the most miserable form of following the crowd.
Especially under the boom created by James Brown Scott.
I fear that even Gurian would be too intelligent to join in.
All the more eager, therefore, are our home-grown beneficiaries of the psychosis of 1945.
You compare my situation to Rossini being booed. That is not right. Today, the press pronounces the defamations and death sentences; the courts of the state merely carry them out.

My brother thinks Captiva Captivitas is far better and much more worth reading than Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen, precisely because Jünger was never a prisoner. The Pour le Mérite has already found its new forms, and Kierkegaard said all of this clearly enough back in 1848.

Since 1936 I have been through terrible things, and several times I have been swallowed by the Leviathan that was already the object of my scholarly observation and research—and which, because of these experiences, became even more so. Being hunted for years as the quarry has made me somewhat tired. But I am still able to tell right from wrong, which my persecutors apparently can no longer do. I am also still able to classify my hunter in conceptual terms.

The ugly deception involved in my first attempt at marriage: is there a parallel between that and the self-deception involved in working with Frank? Or was the deception itself only a side effect of some secret desire to deceive myself? A desire to make myself cheap? An inability to deceive and disappoint other people? A helplessness against being steamrolled by people making brazen demands on me?
Was I too weak to find the courage to disappoint others? That false pity for the fraudster whose fraud I had already seen through? That terrible pity for an offer that nobody accepts?

Why do I feel such terrible pity for the little shopkeeper who waits in vain for a customer, while the customer who asks in vain for goods leaves me indifferent—even though we ourselves were always on the customer’s side?

Can this be a psychological accident, some lingering effect of the sad look I saw on the face of a small shopkeeper when I was a child? Or does it come from realizing that the merchant is now falling victim to the very risk he trusted in—from a deep sense that he is the victim of the supposed free market and its deceptions, that buying is better than selling, that money—until the next currency reform—is better than goods?
All of this shows just how many insights, experiences, diagnoses, calculations, and predictions can be packed into feelings of this kind.
Theodor Haecker, Kierkegaard’s Hump, with a foreword by Richard Seewald, Zurich, Thomas Verlag, Anno Domini MCMXLVII. So that was the secret at the heart of it all!
Kierkegaard had a hump, and Theodor Haecker’s final word on Kierkegaard is about that hump—and about the spirit that the hump built for itself.

On top of this comes a clumsy introduction by the editor of this little book about the hump, Richard Seewald, a bad pseudo-modern painter who places Theodor Haecker’s broken nose beside Kierkegaard’s hump.

So at last we have the thorn in the flesh of these merciless spirits, these radical and demanding polemicists: the secret that was successfully kept quiet for a hundred years, the hidden engine behind this whole extraordinary intellectual existence, the secret motor of this existentialism!
Theodor Haecker’s last word concerns Kierkegaard’s hump!
Si tacuisset, magnus Ironicus mansisset: if he had kept silent, he would have remained a great ironist.

(But I have become so sensitive to polemics that, for me, every o si tacuisset—every “if only he had kept silent”—falls back on the person who says it to someone else. That was precisely the troubling thing about Kierkegaard: his silence never stopped talking.)

With this final word, Theodor Haecker meant only to strike at the non-Catholic—or not-yet-Catholic—Kierkegaard: the radical polemicist, the lover of the absurd, the intolerant Protestant. And Haecker meant well. He handled it tactfully. He was entirely right to qualify how much importance should be attached to the hump. But none of that helps him. He revealed the hump. An act like Ham exposing his father—here, his furious father.
Oh, if only he had kept silent.
I know my age. Simply naming this pudendum, this shameful bodily secret, destroys the Kierkegaard myth, which was already almost complete.
I know the spirit of this age.

With the best intentions, Haecker has tactlessly handed Kierkegaard over to his real enemy, the gutter press, for a second and even worse time. This time it will not be open mockery and ridicule. It will be the certain triumph not only of every psychoanalyst, but of every researcher of mind, body, and soul; every Nietzschean; every eugenicist and biologist; every believer in physical form—and above all that whole mass of educated people who can no longer look past the shape of the body.
And, speaking in Catholic terms, they are even right.

A hump does, after all, create an irregularitas ex defectu corporis propter deformitatem (Canon 984)—an irregularity arising from bodily defect because of deformity—though we need not argue over whether it was a gravior defectus, a more serious defect.
“Only where there are graves are there resurrections” (Nietzsche). Is that supposed to mean that where there are crematoria and urns of ashes there can be no resurrection?
Burning, cremation, means destroying the possibility of resurrection.
Would Nietzsche have allowed himself to be buried?
“For rebirth, the legal principle of the Roman-Jewish spirit is a greater obstacle than the Satanic” (Walter Schubart, Dostoevsky and Nietzsche, 1939).
So that, then, would be the enemy. Bruno Bauer comes close to it.
“Life draws strength from the spring of evil; better evil than the bourgeois middle ground”—that is Nietzsche, and Schubart agrees with him in Dostoevsky’s name.
“But it is not in our power to decide what enters our consciousness and what does not” (W. Schubart).
For all the people who write diaries:
My diary purrs As the roasting spit turns: Nothing fills up more easily Than a calendar.
([Goethe,] Sayings in Rhyme, Tame Xenien IV).
